title: Compare and Contrast Wireless Security Protocols and Authentication Methods

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Wireless security asks two different questions: how the radio traffic is protected, and how the user or device proves its identity.
bullets: Protocols and encryption: WPA2, WPA3, TKIP, AES
Authentication: RADIUS, TACACS+, Kerberos, multifactor authentication

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Distinguish the protocol or encryption protecting wireless traffic from the service or method authenticating a user or administrator.
sections.callout: Protect the radio traffic → authenticate the user or device.

entries.title: Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2)
paragraphs: An established and still common wireless security generation, strongly associated with AES-based protection.
entries.recognitionCue: Established secure Wi-Fi with AES → WPA2.

entries.title: WPA3
paragraphs: The newer wireless security generation with improved protections and the preferred choice when supported.
entries.recognitionCue: Newer and stronger WPA generation → WPA3.

entries.title: Temporal Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP)
paragraphs: A legacy encryption technology associated with earlier WPA deployments; it is not the preferred modern option.

entries.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
paragraphs: A strong symmetric encryption standard used for modern wireless protection.

sections.title: WPA2 vs. WPA3

table.caption: Wireless security generations
rows: Established, common, and associated with AES
Newer generation with improved security capabilities

sections.callout: If all devices support it and the question asks for the newer generation, choose WPA3.

sections.title: TKIP vs. AES
sections.callout: WPA2 and WPA3 are protocol generations; TKIP and AES are encryption technologies.

sections.title: Authentication
paragraphs: Authentication establishes whether a user, device, or administrator should receive access.

entries.title: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS)
paragraphs: Provides centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting for network access and is commonly used by enterprise Wi-Fi and VPN services.
entries.recognitionCue: Users or devices joining a network → RADIUS.

entries.title: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+)
paragraphs: Centralizes administrative authentication and authorization for network infrastructure such as routers and switches.
entries.recognitionCue: Administrator logging into a router or switch → TACACS+.

entries.title: Kerberos
paragraphs: A ticket-based authentication protocol strongly associated with Active Directory domain authentication.

entries.title: Multifactor Authentication
paragraphs: Requires more than one factor category, such as a password plus a token or a PIN plus a fingerprint.

table.caption: Choose the authentication system from the scenario

Domain tickets for identities and resources

sections.title: Wireless Security Decision Model
bullets: If the question asks for a Wi-Fi security generation, choose between WPA2 and WPA3.
If it asks which encryption protects the traffic, choose between legacy TKIP and modern AES.
If enterprise users are authenticating to network access, think RADIUS.
If administrators are authenticating to network devices, think TACACS+.
If the clue is a domain ticket, think Kerberos.
If the clue is multiple factor categories, think multifactor authentication.

sections.title: Objective 2.3 Exam Trap
bullets: WPA2 is a wireless security protocol; AES is an encryption algorithm.
WPA3 is newer than WPA2; WPA2 remains common.
TKIP is legacy; AES is modern and stronger.
RADIUS authenticates network access; TACACS+ commonly authenticates network-device administrators.
RADIUS centralizes network entry; Kerberos uses domain authentication tickets.
Encryption protects traffic; authentication verifies identity.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: Protect the radio traffic → authenticate the user.
